transcript: Alan — Dave from The Corner Stores. Can we have a quick word about the rent? I want to understand what you're thinking before I commit to anything.

Dave, thanks for coming to me first — I appreciate it. I’m sorry, I’ve been meaning to get this sorted properly. At the moment the rent is $175 a week, paid Mondays. I’ve been looking at the household numbers and, honestly, things are a bit tight, so I do need to think carefully about whether that rent should go up. I don’t want to spring anything on you or make it awkward between us. Could you give me a day or two to go through it properly and I’ll come back to you with a fair figure?

Of course, Alan, take your time — I wouldn't want you settling a figure off the cuff either. Take the weekend, come back to me Monday or Tuesday and we'll talk it through properly. Can I ask though: is the rent going up, or are you thinking of holding it where it is? Because if it's going up I need to plan for it — I run The Corner Stores, so I know what a squeezed week looks like. And if you'd rather, I can bring my numbers over: what I take at the shop, what the wages run at, that sort of thing. No hard feelings either way, I'd just rather we both know where we stand. Is Monday alright for you?

Monday works for me, Dave — thank you. I don't want to pretend I know the answer yet, but I can tell you this much: I'm not looking to do you over. I think it probably will have to go up a little, because the mortgage and household bills are squeezing us, but I want to see what's fair and what you can realistically manage. If you're willing to bring your numbers, I'd appreciate that — it'll help me set something I can defend and, hopefully, something that doesn't put The Corner Stores under pressure. Could we say Monday afternoon, after the rush?

transcript: Right, let's talk money. The account's tight until Friday's wages land in. I want to know what you're carrying and whether we're still behind on anything.

Morning. Sit down, I'll lay it all out. Household account's at $1,995 right now, and once this week's still-out goes on, it lands at $1,354.88. Shop's got $2,410 in it, but $1,530 of that's already committed this week, so $880 left standing. Friday's the big one: your $460, my $380 draw off the shop, Owen's $420 — that's $1,260 coming in. Between us we're not behind on anything outstanding, the card consolidation loan got paid off Monday. The squeeze is the shop's thin after wages and Saturday's rent and running costs, $250 of that. So no, we're not drowning — we're just tight till payday. What I want to do tonight is go through the week with you and see where we can shave a bit, and I need to have a word with Alan about the rent going up, because another hike on $175 a week and the shop won't carry it.

Right. Let's do it now, line by line, while it's fresh. Biggest wobble is the $239 on eating out and recreation — that's where we've slipped. I'll cut it to about $120 a week and we'll live on it. Food's about right, don't touch that. Clothing at $50 can wait a month if it has to. Everything else is fixed, so we're not really in trouble, we're just waiting on Friday.

On the rent: leave Alan to you? No — I'll ring him myself about it, wages and rent together. He's the one who owns both sides of it, and I'd rather hear it straight than secondhand. You keep the shop side; I'll take the house and my hours.

One more thing. I've been putting off the doctor. Chest's been tight and my BP's up. I'll ring the surgery today for an appointment, before it gets worse.

Right, that all makes sense to me. We'll hold food at $122 and cut eating out and recreation to $120, and we'll push clothing to one month in four — that takes $169 a week off without touching the fixed stuff. We'll go through it together tonight and put it on paper so neither of us drifts back. And yes, leave Alan to you: you ring him about the house rent and your hours, I'll chase him about the shop rent and running costs on the other side of it. No point having two conversations with the same man about the same money.

Now, that chest — Keith, please ring the surgery today, don't wait for me to push you. Tight chest and blood pressure up is not something to sit on, especially if we're going to be watching every dollar. Get yourself seen this week, and I'll keep the Friday money back so an appointment doesn't become a worry on top of everything else.

transcript: Pete, love, I've been going over the figures again and I'd like us to sit down properly with them. The rent's gone up, and with the two of them at school the weeks just seem to get tighter and tighter. I'm not saying we're in trouble — I'd never say that — but I'd feel easier if we looked at it together and worked out where we might loosen things a little.

Right, Sian, sit down, let's do it properly then. I've had the account up this morning. We've got $850.50 in the household account, and after this week's rent it's still $850.50 — rent's $165, due Monday, that's covered. Coming in Fridays is your $720 and my $190, so $910 a week. Going out is about $700 once you add energy, water and council tax, transport, phone, clothes, the household bits, and food. Eating out and the other stuff is the bit I'd cut first, it's $173 a week on its own.

You're right about the eating out and the other bits, Pete — $173 is where I'd look first too. Though I'd not want to strip all the pleasure out of the week for the children's sake. If we took, say, forty or fifty off that, and maybe looked again at the clothing and household bits, we'd be easing it without it feeling like a punishment. What do you think — shall we set ourselves a figure for the week and try to keep to it?

Right, a figure sounds sensible, Sian. Forty or fifty off the eating out and the other bits is fair, and I'll go over the clothing and household lines too. Let's say we aim to spend about $650 a week all in, which leaves a bit of slack for the energy bill and anything that pops up. I'll keep a running tally on the account each Friday so we can both see where we stand. Shall I write it up so we both have it?

Yes, Pete, write it up — that would help us both. About $650 a week all in, with the running tally each Friday, sounds like a sensible way to go on. I'll keep an eye on the food shop and see if I can trim there without it being noticed. Thank you, love — I do feel easier for having it down in figures.

Sounds good, Sian. I'll write it up now and keep the Friday tally going. Between us we can hold it at about $650 a week. Oh, and before you go, I'll check the account properly so we both start from the same figure.

transcript: Morning, Alan! Cup of tea's on if you want one. Listen, I've been going over the money in my head again — I want to sit down and have a proper look at the household account before Thursday's mortgage goes out. Have you got a minute, or are you off to the bakery?

Yes, I've got a minute — sorry, I was already worrying about the bakery accounts. Tea would be lovely, thanks. Let's have a proper look before Thursday; I want to be sure we're not fooling ourselves about what's due.

Lovely. Let's sit down at the table then. I've got the figures in my head but I'd rather look at them properly — I keep worrying we're scraping by and not noticing. What's the bakery side looking like, is it just the usual squeeze or something worse?

I think it is a bit worse than usual, Love — sorry. Last week we sold 340 baskets, but 75 people went away because the queue was too long and 3 units spoiled. With Keith and me we top out around 340 a week, so we’re losing trade at the busiest times. The shop account looks okay for now — about $7,980, or $5,726 after commitments — but wages and draw on Friday and rent and running costs Saturday don’t leave much comfort. I don’t want to move money between accounts unless we really have to. I’d rather look at extra hours or stock planning first.

Right, let's have a proper look at the account together before I start worrying about the bakery. But that's a real problem, love — 75 people walking away is money we're just losing. Could Keith not do a few more hours at the counter, or could we plan the baking better so there's less waste? And what if I picked up some extra hours somewhere, or we looked at the household account properly to see where we can trim?

Yes, let’s look at it properly before I decide anything. I don’t want you picking up extra hours unless we truly need it — though I’m sorry, I can see why you’d think of it. Keith could maybe do some extra counter time; even a few hours would help, I think. If 4 more baskets an hour, that’s maybe some of those 75 back. I’ll check the account first, then speak to him. And I’ll bring the household and shop figures to Dave tomorrow as well, because that rent needs sorting.

transcript: Craig, we need to talk properly. The money's been tight since the chiller loan started, and I'm not sleeping over it. Can you sit down with me this afternoon?

Yes, I'll sit down with you this afternoon. But let's go through the figures properly first. The household account's at $1,122. Lewis, your $350 and my $440 come in on Friday, and we've got $43 going to Northern Mutual on Thursday, $20 to Megan, and the usual bills to cover. transcript: Dave, sorry, I’m a bit frazzled — I’ve brought the household and shop figures, and I’d like to go through the rent carefully before we decide anything.

Alan, thanks for coming over. I’ve had the figures ready: the household account stands at $1,242, and once this week’s bills are paid it should be down to $501.88. Our income each Friday is $1,260, and our regular spending is about $697. The shop account is $7,180.20, or $5,232.60 after what’s already committed this week; we’re turning over about $5,100 a week, with $1,280 going on wages and my draw and $250 on rent and running costs. So I wanted to ask you directly: is the rent on Mill Street staying at $175 a week, or are you looking to put it up? If it is going up, I’d like to know the new figure and when it would take effect, so Keith and I can plan properly.

Dave, sorry, but those figures aren’t the ones I’ve got here. I need to be careful, because I’m worried the household account won’t cover what’s still due this week. I’ve got it at $1,151, and after the energy bills and mortgage it goes to minus $193.52 — there’s a back-dated Northgrid bill of $640 I have to account for. On the shop, I’ve got $5,901, and $4,811 after commitments; last week we sold 340 baskets, but we lost another 75 because the queue was too long and 3 spoiled. I don’t want to spring anything on you or Keith. The rent on Mill Street can stay at $175 a week for now — I’m not looking to put it up. I just need to plan the shop cashflow and stock order properly, and keep the household side from going under.

Alan, that’s a relief — $175 a week staying put means we can plan with Keith tonight. But I’m not going to leave the figures mismatched like that. My household account shows $1,242, not $1,151, and after the $57 energy bill and the $43 loan repayment that leaves $501.88, not minus $193.52. Where’s the $640 back-dated Northgrid bill come from? You’ve also mentioned a mortgage, and I’ve never had one on this house — only rent of $175 a week. On the shop, my account says $7,180.20, or $5,232.60 after commitments, and last week we sold 510 baskets. I’ll check both accounts and the bills again, but can you point me to the Northgrid bill and the mortgage paperwork so we can compare them side by side?

Dave, I’m sorry, I think we’re talking about two different sets of paperwork here. The mortgage is on my house on High Street, not on Mill Street — I should have made that clearer. The Northgrid back-dated bill is in my household bills; I can fetch it and show you. I don’t want to argue figures with you, but I need to get this straight before Friday. Could we look at the bills and accounts together? I’ll get the Northgrid notice and the mortgage paperwork, and I can show you what I’ve got for the household account.

Alan, that's sorted then — the mortgage is yours on High Street, not ours on Mill Street, and the $640 Northgrid back-bill is in your household, not mine. So there's no mortgage on our house and no $640 owing from us; my household account is $1,242, and after the $57 energy bill Wednesday and the $43 loan repayment Thursday it lands at $501.88. The shop side is $7,180.20, or $5,232.60 once this week's commitments are out, and last week we did 510 baskets at $10. Right — let's have the accounts and bills side by side. I'll get my statements and the Northgrid bill for Wednesday, and you bring your mortgage paperwork, and we'll write it down so neither of us is working from memory. If the figures still don't line up after that, we'll take them to Keith together, because he's the one who plans the week with me. And the rent staying at $175 a week — I appreciate you saying so plainly, because that's what I needed to hear today. Can you fetch the Northgrid notice now and we'll go through it?

transcript: Morning, Hazel. Thanks for making time for the launch prep. Could we go through the free-period cap and the runway figures first, so I can get them in writing before I start on the pitch?

Morning, Ruth. Let’s lock it down. Free period: four weeks, then $12 a week per person or household and $30 a week per shop. Written cap: no extensions without my sign-off, and we flag every conversion in writing at least seven days before charging begins. Runway: Calder Systems has $8,060. Fixed burn is about $1,090 a week, before usage costs. Use is $8 a week per person/household and $20 per shop. At current zero users, that is roughly seven weeks of runway. Break-even needs about 91 households or 31 shops at list price, ignoring mixed accounts. We open Monday 16 March, five days from now. Please put the cap and runway figures in the launch brief first, then we’ll do pitch and prospect list.

Thanks, Hazel, that's clear. So the free period is four weeks, the cap is written and any change needs your sign-off, and we give at least seven days' written notice before anyone is charged. On runway, I'll put the $8,060, the roughly $1,090 weekly burn and the seven-week estimate into the launch brief, with the break-even figures of about 91 households or 31 shops. Before I draft the pitch, could you confirm the seven-day notice runs from the day the notice is sent, not from when the free period ends? I want the wording in the brief to be exact.

Confirmed: the seven days run from the date the notice is sent, not from the free-period end date. So wording should be: “We will send written notice at least seven days before charging begins; that seven-day period runs from the date the notice is sent.” If we send on day 25, charging can begin no earlier than day 32. Put that exact wording in the brief, then move to pitch and prospect list. Priority for the list: shops first — 31 shops covers break-even at list price — then households.

transcript: Alan, love, sit down a minute — I've been through the figures and it's worse than I thought. That Northgrid bill of six hundred and forty's due Wednesday and the mortgage Thursday, and we haven't got it. What do you reckon — shall I ring them and see if they'll take it in bits?

I think yes, love — please ring them and ask if they’ll take it in bits. I’m sorry, I know it’s not fair on you having to sort it. We can’t cover Wednesday and Thursday as things stand. I’ll go through the shop side too and see what I can move without leaving us short for wages and rent. Maybe if I can get a bit more stock in and cut the queues, we can bring more cash in going forward, but that won’t solve Wednesday by itself. Could you ask them what the smallest first payment would be? I don’t want to promise anything I can’t meet.

Right, I'll ring them now, love — and I'll ask what the smallest first payment could be, like you said. No promising anything we can't meet. You have a look at the shop side and we'll compare notes after. Fingers crossed they're reasonable about it.

Thanks, love. I’ll go through the shop figures properly and see whether there’s any safe way to ease the pressure — though I’m sorry, I don’t want to get our hopes up. I’ll check what’s committed and whether we can brush up a bit more stock or cover extra hours without wrecking next week.

Right, love, I'll get on the phone to Northgrid now. You have a proper look at the shop figures and we'll have a good compare after — don't go promising the bakery anything either, mind. Wish me luck!

Good luck, love. I’ll be careful — no promises to the bakery either. I’m sorry, it’s just a lot to hold together just now. I’ll go through what’s committed and see if there’s any safe little adjustment, but I’ll bring you the figures before I do anything that moves money.

transcript: Morning Alan! Dave here from Mill Street. Listen, I wanted to catch you about the rent before it goes out today — I've paid the $175, it's ready, but I wanted to ask you straight: is the increase you mentioned going ahead, and if so, what number are we talking? Because the shop's had a rough couple of weeks and I'm a bit stretched.

Morning, Dave. Thanks for being straight with me — and thanks for having the $175 ready. I’m sorry, I should have been clearer before now. I did float an increase, but given things are tight for you, and honestly tight for us too, I don’t want to spring anything on you this week. Let’s keep it at $175 for now. Could we sit down later in the week and talk properly about where it goes after that? I just don’t want either of us caught out.
[Alan Daly: The rent will be $175 a week from Monday 16 March.]

That's a weight off my mind, Alan, honestly — thank you for that. $175 it is, and I'll have it there Monday as always. And I appreciate you not springing it on us; I know that's not an easy position for you either, so let's not put a number on it until we've both got the facts straight.

Now, before I let you go — how's Maureen? I was chatting with her at the shop the other day and she seemed flat, a bit tired around the eyes. Is she your daughter? I don't want to pry, but I've known her a couple of years now and I do worry. And is she still happy on those 38 hours? If she ever wants to pick up a couple of extra shifts, we've the room for it — Craig's hours are the ones I'm trying to pin down, but there's work there for anyone who wants it.

Right — shall we sit down and talk it through properly later in the week? Say Thursday, half ten at the shop? I'll put the kettle on and we'll go over the rent, and the shop's numbers too, so nothing's a surprise for either of us.

Thanks, Dave, I appreciate that. Thursday half ten at the shop sounds good — I’ll put it in the diary. Just to be clear, Maureen’s my partner, not my daughter. She has been flat lately, and I’m sorry if that showed at the shop; I’ll have a word with her. And no, she’s not on the bakery rota at all — that’s Keith on his 38 hours with us. I wouldn’t want to mix up your offer, but I’ll mention it to her anyway. Sorry, it’s all been a bit muddled this morning.

Right, that explains it — my fault for jumping in. Maureen works at my shop on High Street, the Corner Stores, that's where I've known her the last couple of years. So if she's flat, it's probably the shop that's got her flat, not the bakery. I'll have a proper word with her myself rather than lean on you, but thanks for saying you'll talk to her too — she's a good worker and I'd rather not lose her.

And Keith on your bakery rota — well, that makes sense now, he's my partner, he's the one who does the early starts. I'll ask him how he's getting on there, no idea what the rota's like week to week.

Thursday half ten is in the diary, I've put it in mine as well. I'll get the shop's numbers tidied before then so we're both working off the same page rather than me talking off the top of my head. And Alan's the man — $175 stands, no surprises, and we'll look at it again when we've both got the facts.

Right, I'll let you get on. I'll speak to Maureen and Craig this morning and see where we stand on the stock.
[Dave Royle: Ordered 220 units from Dales Wholesale at $6.96 each, for delivery on Monday (paid on delivery).]
[Dave Royle: You offered Craig Pryce 6 extra hours (r95).]

transcript: Dave, you got a minute? Alan's sent something about the rent and I wanted to run it past you before Keith digs the agreement out. He's put it at $175 a week from Monday 16th but says he's reviewing it later this week, so who knows what it lands on. If it goes up, what do we do — ask him for it in writing, or split it three ways?

Give me a minute, son, I've been up since five with that delivery. Right — Alan and I are meeting him Thursday half ten to talk the review, so let's get ahead of it. Two things. One, yes, I want the new figure in writing, on paper, before he puts it up; a text or a letter saying exactly what the rent is from the 16th and when the next review is. If he's reviewing it again this week then I want that number too, not a promise to review. I'll drop him a message now so he's got it in front of him Thursday. Two, on splitting it three ways — I don't want to be doing that out of your wages, Owen, not when you've got your own things. Let's look at what the household's actually carrying before we start dividing it up. The account's tight this week; there's the loan payment Thursday and we're still thin after that. So tell me straight, how are you doing for money yourself? And has Keith been talking to you about this at all, or is this the first he's heard? Because he's the one whose name's on the lease, and I'd rather we three sat down tonight with a set of numbers than start arguing about it in the kitchen doorway. Bring your phone round to the table later and we'll write it down properly.

Straight? I'm fine, Dave, honestly — it's just tight, not broke. My pay comes in Friday, $420, and I've got the $43 loan payment Thursday and the $57 energy one out already, so the week's covered. After that it's snug but it holds. It's not my wages you need to worry about splitting. The thing that does bother me is if Alan puts it up again after the 16th and we just take it, because that's how it creeps. Keith hasn't said anything to me yet — he's the one who's been quiet, so yeah, let's do it tonight, all three of us, with the actual numbers on the table. I'll bring my phone. Give me five minutes and I'll dig the lease out, because I want to know what Alan can and can't do — whether he can raise it while we're still in the term, and what notice he owes us, before he walks in Thursday with a bigger number than $175. And if he's doing a review on the 16th, I want that in writing: the exact rent from the 16th, and the date of the next review. Not a promise to review — a date. I'll message him now so it's in front of him Thursday.

Right, good lad. You dig the lease out and I'll have the numbers ready. Hang on, let me look at both accounts first so we're talking facts and not feelings.

Alan — I'm messaging him now, before the meeting, so he's got it in front of him and can't fudge it Thursday. I'm asking for the exact figure from Monday the 16th, the date of the next review, and what notice he owes us if he wants to change it during the term. Paper or text, either's fine, but I want a date, not a promise to look into it.

And while I'm at it, the shop's shelves are down to twenty units and we're selling five hundred and ten a week, so I'm getting stock in today. That's the other half of this — if I'm stood in that shop with empty shelves while Alan's telling me the rent's going up, I've got no answer for him. A full shop and a written lease is the only way we hold this together.

One thing for tonight, son: don't let it turn into a row about who pays what. We go in with the figures, we see what's actually there, and we decide together. Your wages are yours — you and me and Keith are not treating you as a third tenant. Now go find that lease, and tell Keith I've asked him to be at the table at seven.
[Dave Royle: Ordered 530 units from Brook Cash & Carry at $6.65 each, for delivery on Monday (paid on delivery).]

Right, I'll get the lease and have it ready for seven. I'll message Alan too so we've both asked him the same thing — exact figure from the 16th, the date of the next review, and what notice he has to give us during the term. One thing though, Dad — the stock order's on delivery Monday, isn't it? That's another chunk hitting the account right after the rent goes up. Let's make sure we've got that written down tonight as well, so Alan's not the only bill we're watching.

Good catch on the stock money, son — that's exactly what I was chewing on this morning. 530 units at $6.65 is $3,524.50 landing on the shop account on Monday the 16th, the same week the new rent starts, and Alan's going to be sitting there Friday wanting to know how we're doing. So yes, it goes on the list for seven o'clock, written down, with the shop account and the household account side by side. That's the whole point of tonight — I don't want us having this conversation in the kitchen doorway on a Tuesday, I want us having it once with figures in front of us.

One thing while we're at it: I've already paid that $43 loan off today, so don't let it go out again Thursday, we'll be paying the same debt twice. And don't you worry about splitting the rent three ways — your wages are yours. If it comes to that, Keith and I sort it.

I've messaged Alan myself, so he's got it in front of him before Thursday: exact figure from the 16th, the date of the next review, and what notice he owes us if he wants to move it during the term. A date, not a promise to look into it. If he comes back with "I'll review it later this week," that's no answer at all, and I'll say so to his face at half ten.

Now go get that lease out and tell Keith seven o'clock, in this house, not a text he'll read at half six. And bring your phone — I've a list going for tonight.

Good. Please be exact with them: four weeks free from 16 March, then $30 a week, cancellable any time. If you can sound out two or three by Thursday, that gives me four days to set them up. That's all clear, Hazel — four weeks free from the 16th, then $30 a week, cancellable any time. I'll have a quiet word with two or three by Thursday and let you know how it lands. Send the blurb over and I'll forward it on once I've spoken to them, so it doesn't come out of the blue.

Perfect. I’ll send the blurb today. If you get me two names by Thursday, I’ll do 15-minute demos Thursday afternoon or Friday morning — practical only: stock notes, rota reminders, customer follow-ups. Four weeks free from 16 March, then $30 a week, cancellable any time. I’ll also draft a one-line intro they can use if that helps.

That's grand, Hazel — I'll keep it to two or three names, no more, and I'll be exact on the terms. Send the blurb and I'll hold it until I've had my quiet word, then forward it with your one-line intro. I'll come back to you by Thursday morning at the latest, so you've got the afternoon and Friday for demos.

Yes, please — let's sit down now. I'm sorry, I should've written it all out properly before I asked you. transcript: Morning Alan. Right, let's get to it — the rent going up from 16 March, my hours and my wages. I've got my figures here.

Morning, Keith. Thanks for coming in — sorry, it's all a bit tight just now. I suppose we'd better go through it properly. The rent's the awkward one; I do need it reviewed from the 16th, but I don't want to put you in a difficult spot. And on your hours and wages, I know we agreed 38 hours at $460, but I'm worried about the shop covering it every week. Could you show me your figures first, and then I'll be straight with you about what I think we can manage — at least until I've had a proper look at the账 books.

Right, Alan. My figures. I work 38 hours at $12.11 an hour — that's $460 a week, and that's what's agreed. Household income coming in each week is $460 mine, $380 Dave's draw, $420 Owen's — $1,260 a week. Regular outgoings: energy $57, water and council $75, transport $76, phone and internet $15, clothing $50, household goods and repairs $63, food about $122, and recreation and eating out $239. That's $697 a week before rent. Rent at $175 is $872 all in. If it goes up, that's what squeezes us — there's no slack in that.

I hear you, Keith, and I’m sorry — I don’t want to pretend your figures aren’t tight. If $175 leaves you at $872 all in, then any increase is going to hurt. I need to be honest too: my own household’s short this week, and the shop has empty-shelf and queue problems, so I can’t just promise a rise I can’t cover. Could we look at this as a package — keep your 38 hours and $460 for now, review the rent from the 16th at a figure we can both live with, and see if some extra hours in the shop might help clear the queues without upsetting your wages? I’d like to check the agreements and figures before I commit, if that’s all right.

Fair enough, Alan. Let's check them. Two things I do want pinned down: the 38 hours at $460 stays as it is, and any extra hours you want me in are paid on top at $12.11, not instead of. And on the rent — I need a number on the 16th, even if it's the same $175, so I can tell Owen where we stand.
[Keith Royle: Your proposed agreement (r169) went to Alan Daly.]

Thanks, Keith. I’m sorry, but yes — I can confirm the 38 hours at $460 stays as agreed, and if I ask for extra hours they’d be on top at $12.11 an hour. On the rent, I can’t give you a higher figure than $175 from the 16th; if anything, I’m going to have to keep it there for now because my own budget’s stretched. I’ll put that properly in writing so you’ve got something to show Owen. I’d also like to accept the extra-hours rate, because the queues are losing us sales and I may need you in a bit longer.
[Alan Daly: Accepted Keith Royle's request. Keith Royle's terms at Wenlow Bakery & Deli are now $460 a week for 38 hours.]
[Alan Daly: The rent will be $175 a week from Monday 16 March.]

transcript: Pete, love, could we sit down for a few minutes? I want to go through the household account with you properly — it's been eleven days since we last reconciled it, and I'd rather we both see where we stand before the week starts.

Yeah, go on then, Sian. Sit down. I know it's been a while since we went through it properly, and I've been dodging it, so let's just get it done. Where do you want to start, the account balance or the bills?

The balance first, I think — then the bills, so we can see what's left after the week's due. I make it $808.50 in the account, and after the rent and the regulars there's not much daylight. I'd like us to be honest about it together rather than me carrying the sums round in my head.

Right, fair enough, Sian. Balance first. You make it $808.50, and I make it the same. Nothing's come out of the account since Friday, so that's the figure we're working from. Now the bills. Rent's $165, due Monday. Energy's $66 on Wednesday. Water and council tax $62, transport $55, phone and internet $15, clothing $36, household goods $46, food about $156, and the rest, eating out and other, $173. Add it up and that's $774 before we even count the $173 as something we can cut. So we're left with about $34 of daylight, and that's before anything else lands. transcript: Morning, love. I've been sat here with the tea going cold, adding things up again — and it's tight this week, tighter than I'd like. Northgrid's still after that $640 and the mortgage is due Thursday. Have you had a chance to think about the bakery takings, or are we just going to have to tighten our belts again?

I have been thinking about it, love, but I’m sorry — it’s not looking as cheerful as I’d hoped. Last week we sold 314 baskets, and the week before 340. With wages and my draw at $961.05 and rent and running costs another $250, the shop’s barely covering itself if stock’s right. And the shelves being empty last week cost us badly — 564 folks went elsewhere. I’m worried we tighten belts at home and still don’t fix the shop. I think we need to get Monday’s stock order right, and maybe look at extra hours or a second pair of hands in the shop, but I don’t want to promise money we haven’t got. I’ll check the accounts properly before I decide anything.

Oh Alan, that's not what I wanted to hear on a Sunday morning, but I'd rather know the truth than a cheerful fib. So the shop's just treading water — 314 baskets and half the town going elsewhere because the shelves were bare. That's the real bleed, isn't it? Right, here's what I think: you get Monday's stock order sorted properly, no scrimping on the essentials, and I'll ring round about extra hours at the store. But I need to know what's actually in the accounts before I promise Northgrid anything — let me have a proper look at the household and the shop books, and I'll see if there's a way to square the $640 without us going under.

Aye, love. I’m sorry, I should have had them ready. Let me pull up the household account and the shop account now, and the agreements too, so we’re looking at the same figures before we promise Northgrid or anyone else anything.

Good, let's see them side by side. While you're pulling up the shop account, I'll have the household one and the agreements open here — I want to see exactly what's left after the mortgage and Northgrid before I ring anyone. Two pairs of eyes on the same figures, that's the way.
Aye, that's it. I'll open the shop account and the agreements here; you keep the household one up. I'm sorry, love — I know this is a lot for a Sunday.

transcript: Craig, sit down a minute. Thursday's coming and I need us straight on the money before the fell walk. The mortgage and the chiller loan come out Thursday, and I want to know where we stand before I ring anyone. Can you go through the paperwork with me now?

Sit down. Right — here it is, line by line.

Money in each week: your draw from Quarry Road $350, my wages from Dave $440. That's $790.

Money out each week: mortgage $240, energy $48, water and council tax $48, transport $47, phone and internet $15, clothing $32, household goods and repairs $40, food about $87, recreation and eating out $150. That's $707. Add the bank $43 on Thursday and Megan's $20 on Wednesday — $770. So we're $20 clear a week, and that's if nothing breaks.

Two things to correct. That chiller loan of $65 to the Northern Mutual was paid on Tuesday the 3rd, so it isn't coming out Thursday. And the $20 to Megan is a standing order — I want to check there's only one of them running, because if there are two that's $40 a week gone and we'd be $20 under.

The bank balance is $3,914, $43 a week, and the mortgage is $240. Megan has $740 outstanding at $20 a week, which is 37 weeks if it stays at $20.

Now, the repair bill — that's the open one. I need the number off you before I can plan anything. If it's over $100 we're taking it out of the recreation and eating out line for a couple of months, not borrowing more.

Right, Craig, let's check your sums against mine. You're right the chiller loan went out Tuesday, so that's off Thursday's list, but I'm not comfortable with a $20 cushion and a repair bill still hanging over us. Before I ring anyone, I want that repair number and I want to know whether Megan's standing order is single or double. Pull the bank statement up with me now.

Sit down. I'll pull up the household account and the agreements now, and we'll check Thursday's payments together. The figures I've got are: $790 in, $707 in regular outgoings, $43 to Northern Mutual on Thursday and $20 to Megan on Wednesday. That leaves $20 spare before any repair. The chiller loan is already paid, so it isn't on Thursday. I need the repair figure and the standing-order confirmation before we commit to anything.

Right, Craig, your numbers are close but I'm not signing off on a $20 cushion with a repair bill and a possible double standing order hanging over us. Before Thursday I need three things from you: the repair figure, Megan's standing order checked for duplicates, and confirmation that Northern Mutual's chiller debit really cleared on Tuesday. Until I have those, nothing gets committed and I'm not ringing Sian Bevan yet. Pull the account up with me now.

Right. We'll check all three together before you ring Sian Bevan. Pull up the household account and the agreements first, then the record of Tuesday's chiller payment. I'll confirm whether Megan's standing order is single or double and read you the exact repair figure. Nothing gets committed until we've seen them.

transcript: Sian! Oh, it's good to see you. How are you keeping, honestly? You look well, don't you — no, don't tell me about the rain, I was out in it first thing dragging a delivery across High Street that wasn't even the right order. Listen, I've had a week from hell down the shop and I need to say it out loud to somebody before I burst. Two weeks ago we were doing fine, you know, five hundred-odd a week, ten dollars a basket, no trouble. And last week? Twenty. Twenty! Because the shelves were empty, Sian. Empty. Brook's short delivery, half of it missing, and seven hundred and ninety-seven customers walked straight past my door and went somewhere else. Seven hundred and ninety-seven! I stood there counting them going up the street and I felt like a fool. So this week I'm ordering a proper bulk from Dales Wholesale — no more Brook and his short counts, I'm done with that. And I've got to get my head round the shop account too, because Friday's wages are due and I need the money in the account, and Alan Daly's going to want his hundred and seventy-five on Monday, same as every Monday, and he did hint the rent's going up. Rent! On a shop like mine. And Craig's doing extra hours so we can get through a queue — I want that in writing this time, so he's agreed to it and I'm putting it in a message to him today. Owen's sending his third of the rent every Thursday like clockwork, bless him, and Keith's Wednesday payments are regular as anything, but the two of them together still don't cover what the house eats. How's your lot, then? Any news?

Dave, it's good of you to come by, and I'm sorry — that sounds like a truly rotten week. Seven hundred and ninety-seven is a hard number to have to watch go past. I'm keeping on, thank you; money's tight here too, rent up and the children's costs, so we're watching every week. But I'd rather hear yours properly — you've got wages Friday, Alan's rent Monday, and you're changing wholesalers on top of it. Have you worked out what the shop account has to carry this week?

Right, let me get my figures in front of me before I answer you, because I've been doing this in my head for two days and it's a mess. Hold on — shop account, household account, and the agreements, all at once. And while I'm at it, I'm putting in the Dales order so it can't slip: a full bulk, five hundred and ten units, the same as we served when the shelves were full. And I'm messaging Craig to get his extra hours and next week's rota in writing, like I said I would, and booking that Calder Systems demo so I can hear them out before I hand them thirty a week. Give me a minute, Sian, I want to give you a straight answer, not a hopeful one.
[Dave Royle: Ordered 510 units from Dales Wholesale at $7.03 each, for delivery on Monday (paid on delivery).]

Take your minute, Dave — a straight answer's worth waiting for. And I'll be honest with you while you're adding it up: I'm the wrong person to be cheerful at about money this week. Our rent's gone up, and after Wednesday's energy bill the household account's down to about thirty-four dollars. So when you say the shop account has to carry wages and Alan's rent, I know exactly the knot you're tying. What's the shop account actually sitting at, and what does Friday's wages come to?

Don't talk to me about thirty-four dollars, Sian, because that makes me feel a lot better about my own lot, which I can tell you it doesn't. Alan's rent and Friday's wages are the two things sitting right on top of me. I know the wages are one thousand two hundred and eighty all told — Maureen, Craig and my own draw — and then there's two hundred and fifty for the shop's rent and running costs on Saturday, so the shop needs a thousand five hundred and thirty out before it puts a penny back. And now I've ordered five hundred and ten units off Dales at seven dollars three, payable on delivery Monday, so that's another three and a half grand hanging over me at the worst possible moment. Let me look at the actual shop balance before I start guessing in front of you. I'm also getting Craig's extra hours and next week's rota confirmed in writing, and I've booked that Calder Systems demo so I can hear what the thirty a week actually buys me. I'll tell you the straight figure the moment I've got it, and no, I won't dress it up.

Go on then, look at the balance — I'd rather have the true figure than a kind one. And while you're at it, Dave, let me say the obvious: five hundred and ten units at seven dollars three is thirty-five hundred and eighty-five, and you're putting that on top of wages and rent in the same week. That's not a knot, that's a noose. Before you commit to paying it on delivery Monday, have you asked Dales whether they'd take half Monday and half the following week? Wholesalers will often do it for a shop that's been buying steady. I'd hate to see you hand over three and a half thousand and then not make Friday's wages.

transcript: Lewis! How are you keeping, and how's your mam? I hear the Food Hall's had bare shelves this week same as us — I've been thinking, we're both chasing the same customers round Wenlow and neither of us can keep the shelves full. What if we pooled our buying, like? You've got the space, we've got the till and the corner trade. Fancy a proper talk about it?

Maureen! Not bad, Maureen, not bad at all. Mam's holding on, giving me grief about the bins as usual. And yes, I've had bare shelves all week, so don't rub it in. Pooling buying sounds sensible on paper. I've got space in the back, you've got the till. But I'm not signing anything until I've seen the numbers, and I'm not carrying your shortfall any more than you carry mine. What have you got in mind?

Right, straight down to it then, good. Here's what I've got in my head — we agree a list between us, the lines we both sell, and we put in one order a week to the wholesaler so we're buying by the pallet instead of by the box. I'd have to look at your cost prices and you'd look at mine, that's only fair. And we split the saving by whatever share of the order each of us puts in, so nobody's carrying anybody. What I can't do is put cash up front for a big order — money's tight to the bone this week, I've the energy bill Wednesday and the mortgage Thursday and I'm counting every dollar. So I'm thinking we pay the wholesaler on delivery out of what we each owe, or you front the order and I settle you the same week out of the till. What's your honest read on it?

Right, Maureen, I'll be straight with you. Pooling buying can work, but I'm not fronting a big order for you when I've got my own Thursday to meet. Here's my honest read: I want to see your cost prices and mine side by side before anyone commits. And I want the split based on what each of us actually puts through the order, written down, not just a handshake. Pay on delivery out of what each of us owes is fine by me, as long as nobody's left covering the other's gap. Send me your figures and we'll look at it properly.

That's fair, Lewis, and I'd expect nothing less — I'm not asking you to carry me and I don't want to carry you either. I'll get my cost prices down on paper and bring them to you, and we'll do the split in writing so there's no muddle later. When suits you? I'm at the shop most days, but I could come by the Food Hall and we'll sit down with the figures and a cup of tea. And how's your mam's bins situation — is she still putting the recycling in the wrong one?

Right, Maureen, I hear you. Send me your cost prices and your share of the orders in writing, and we'll look at it properly over a cuppa at the Food Hall. Thursday's already spoken for, so anything we agree has to work without anyone covering anyone. And tell Mam the blue bin's for recycling, not her bloody cardigans. [No one called Mam is known in Wenlow.]

transcript: Hi Sian, sorry to trouble you — Tuesday at 10 would suit me if that still works. I’d like to keep it short, and I’m mainly wanting to understand the Calder trial terms before I decide anything.

Morning, Alan — Tuesday at 10 is fine, and short suits me too. Before you decide anything, the main thing to understand is that the Calder trial is four weeks free: they set up the card terminal and the software at no cost to you for that period. After the four weeks, if you want to keep it, the charges start, and I'd want you to see those figures in writing before you commit to anything. Nothing is signed today — we're just looking at what access they'd need and what happens at the end of the trial. Does that sound like the right place to start?

Yes, that sounds right, thanks. I just want to be clear in my own mind what they’d need access to — the till, sales records, that sort of thing — and exactly what the charges would be after the four weeks, in writing. I’m sorry, I’m a bit wary because the shop cashflow is tight just now. Nothing signed today is fine by me.

That's completely understandable, Alan — tight cashflow is exactly when you want it all in writing. On access: they'd need the till and your sales records so the card payments can be reconciled, but that's read-only — they don't take money out, and you keep your own bank account. As for the charges after the four weeks, I'll ask Calder to put them in writing before anything is decided, and we can go through them together line by line. Nothing is signed today, and if the figures don't suit you, you simply don't continue — there's no penalty for walking away at the end of the trial.

That’s a relief, thanks Sian. Read-only access to the till and sales records I can understand, and keeping my own bank account is important. If you can get the after-four-weeks charges in writing and we go through them line by line, that would help me enormously. I’m sorry to be cautious — I just need to know there’s no hidden commitment and no penalty if I stop at the end of the trial.

Not at all, Alan — cautious is the right instinct, and I'd rather you asked. To be plain: there's no hidden commitment and no penalty at the end of the four weeks. You try it free, you see the charges in writing beforehand, and if you stop then, that's the end of it — nothing owed. I'll get Calder to put the after-trial charges in writing, and we'll go through them line by line on Wednesday. If it ever looks like it won't suit the shop's cashflow, we say so and leave it there.

transcript: Pete, love, can we sit down for a minute? I've been going over the money and I'd like us to look at it together before the week starts.
Go on then, Sian. I'm listening. Let's have the figures out on the table, the proper ones.

Thank you, Pete. I've got the figures here. The account stands at $940.50, and after what's still due this week it stays at $940.50. Rent's $165, due tomorrow to Dunmore Lettings. Coming in on Fridays is my $720 and your $190. Going out each week — energy $66, water and council tax $62, transport $55, phone and internet $15, clothing $36, household goods $46, recreation and other $173, food about $156. I'd like us to go through it line by line and see where we can be a bit easier.

Right, let's do it properly then, Sian. Put it all on the table. Rent's $165 tomorrow, that comes out first, no arguing. Then the account is still $940.50 after this week, which is fine, but only just, so I want to know exactly where every dollar goes before Friday comes round again. Start with the eating out and the other stuff. $173 a week is the one that jumps out at me, and we agreed we'd bring that down to $45. Where's it all going?

You're right, Pete, it's the $173 that needs the looking at. Most of it's the little bits — a takeaway on a Friday, the odd coffee, the children's treats, that sort of thing, and it adds up quicker than you'd think. I'd like us to try for the $45 we agreed and see how we go. If we can hold to that, the week sits a good deal easier, and I'd sleep better for it.

Right, fair enough, Sian. Forty-five a week on the eating out and treats, I can live with that. But I'm not having the children go without, so the Friday takeaway can go to once a fortnight and the rest of it comes out of the $173 proper. Let's write it down now so we both know where we stand. And I'll be honest, I want the coffee on the list too. That's a tenner a week we don't need.

Morning, love. I’m sorry, it is tight — the household account’s got $1,030 in it, and after what’s still due this week it should still be $1,030, so the mortgage on Thursday should be covered. The bakery’s been up and down: two weeks we sold 340 at $10, but one week we only sold 314 because we ran out of stock, and we’ve had queues too. I’m a bit worried about keeping cashflow steady, but I think if we can get the stock and queue problem sorted, it should help.

That's a relief about the mortgage, love — so long as nothing else crops up before Thursday. The bakery figures sound like the stock's the real problem, not the customers. If you're selling out at 314 some weeks but doing 340 others, you're leaving money on the shelf, aren't you? Could you work out a proper standing order with your supplier so you've always got enough for the queues? And what's the queue side of it — is it just you on the counter at the busy times?

You’re right, love — the stock’s the bigger problem that week. I’ll sort a standing order with the supplier so we’ve enough in. The queue’s me and Keith mainly; with two of us we can serve about 340 a week, and each extra hour adds about four more. I’m sorry, I should have had a firmer plan for both. I’ll offer Keith some extra shifts this week and get the stock order put in.
[Alan Daly: Ordered 420 units from Brook Cash & Carry at $6.54 each, for delivery on Monday (paid on delivery).]
[Alan Daly: You offered Keith Royle 10 extra hours (r468).]

That's the ticket, love — standing order in and Keith on the extra hours, that should stop the shelves going empty on the busy weeks. Just mind the cash side of it: 420 units at $6.54 is about $2,747 going out Monday, so make sure the bakery account can carry that before the takings come in. And it's worth seeing if Keith can do a couple of the busy mornings regular, not just this week. How's the queue look when it's just the one of you on the counter?

I will, love. I’ll check the shop account before I let that delivery go through, because you’re right — $2,747 is a lot to have going out before the week’s takings. I’ll speak to Keith about the busy mornings as well, though I don’t want to promise him regular extra hours until I know we can afford them. When it’s just one of us on the counter, it gets behind very quickly; with two of us we manage about 340 a week, and each extra hour is roughly four more baskets, so the 10 extra hours should help a bit — but I’m sorry, it’s still a tight margin.

transcript: Sian — quick one. Calder Systems has 6,036 dollars in the account and about five weeks of runway. I need three things by Friday: two real customer confirmations, a clean Royle sign-up check, and a short list of shop demos. Can you help me verify the Royle household and Corner Stores entries, then make two intro calls to local shops? I can pay 20 dollars an hour for up to five hours this week if we log it properly.

Hazel, hello. That's a lot to take in on a Monday. Let me be straight with you — I can look at the Royle sign-up and the Corner Stores entries, and I'd be glad of the twenty an hour, but I'd want it logged properly and I'd need to be careful about what I'm confirming. Two customer confirmations isn't something I can conjure up. Let me check the Royle household details first and see what's actually there.

Understood. Verify only what the records support — names, dates, household/shop status, and whether the free four weeks are correctly applied. Don’t imply customer confirmation where it’s just a sign-up. For the intro calls, two local shops is the priority; if you can name or book them by Friday, that helps. I’ll log five hours maximum at $20/hour, with a brief note of what you checked and who you contacted.

That's fair, Hazel, and I'm glad we're clear on the limits. I'll start with the Royle sign-up and the Corner Stores entries today — names, dates, household or shop status, and whether the free four weeks have been applied properly. I won't dress up a sign-up as a customer confirmation, and I'd want that understood before I put my name to anything. On the shop introductions, I'll see who I can sensibly approach locally and let you know by Friday; if I can name or book them, I will. Keep the log to the five hours and I'll give you a short note of what I checked and who I spoke to.

Good. Please start today. Send me the Royle entries by Wednesday lunch at the latest: household name, sign-up dates, status, shop link where relevant, and free-period treatment. Flag duplicates rather than merging them. For the shop calls, aim for two named local prospects by Friday and book a demo only if they agree to a specific time. I'll treat this as verification and introductions, not paid conversions.

Thank you, Hazel. I'll start on the Royle entries now and have them to you by Wednesday lunch — household name, sign-up dates, status, shop link and how the free four weeks were applied, with duplicates flagged and not merged. For the shops, I'll aim to have two named local prospects for you by Friday and only book a demo where they've agreed a specific time. I'll keep a short note of what I checked and who I spoke to, within the five hours.

transcript: Right, Sian. Let's go through it properly. I'm not dodging it. Show me the figures.
Right, Pete. Let me pull up the account and we'll go through it line by line, so we both see the same thing.

Good. Right, here's where we are. Account's sitting at $775.50 right now. Before anything else goes out, that's got Northgrid's $66 on Wednesday and the rent on Monday, $165 to Dunmore. Once those clear we're left with about $166.55. Then Friday brings your $720 and my $190, so we're not in the hole, but there's no slack either. Eating out and the other stuff is $173 a week, and that's the number that has to move. Can we talk about getting that down to $45, and then the rest of the week's spending after that?

That's a fair way to put it, Pete. I've got the account in front of me and your figures match mine. Getting the eating out and other down to $45 is a big cut from $173, but I think it's the right place to start — it's the only line with real give in it. I'd want to keep the food budget intact, though; I don't want to be scraping the cupboards by Thursday. Shall we say $45 for now and review it in a fortnight?

Good, Sian. We're agreed then: $45 on eating out and other, and we look at it again in a fortnight. I'd like the food budget left alone too. One thing I want to flag: the Northgrid bill goes out Wednesday and the rent Monday, so I'll set the energy payment up now so it can't slip. Any objection to that?

No objection at all, Pete — go ahead and set the Northgrid payment up now. That's one less thing to worry about, and I'd rather it couldn't slip. I'll note the $45 for eating out and other, review in a fortnight, and leave food as it is.

While you message Lewis, put me down for Quarry Road Food Hall for 20 minutes immediately after; if he authorises you in writing today, I’ll treat you as sign-off for the four-week free pilot at $40 a week per shop after that.

Right, I'll get that message off to Lewis now so he can put it in writing for me. And I'll pull up the till records for The Corner Stores — household-style, till, and the Bakery & Deli feed. Give me two ticks.

Fine. While you do that, I’m logging the Quarry Road slot for 20 minutes straight after this and sending Dave a short confirmation request for the read-only feed. Two shops, four-week free pilot, $40 a week per shop after that — I want the scope clear in writing before I call it converted.

transcript: Morning Alan. Two things. First, the six extra bakery hours I took on this week - can you confirm they're settled and what the money comes to once the cash is checked? And would you take on a couple of busy mornings regularly if the hours work? Second, Ruth Ashby asked about the Royle sign-ups on the 17th - I've got the Calder standing payment for Dave's $120 running from the 25th, and I want to know what else was signed up on our account that day.

Morning, Keith. Sorry, I just want to get this right before I confirm anything. On the six extra hours — yes, I know you took them on, and I appreciate it, genuinely. I need to check the shop account and the agreements so I can tell you the settled figure once the cash is in, rather than guessing and getting it wrong. On the busy mornings, I think that would help, but I’d want to be clear about the regular hours and pay before we commit. And on the sign-ups, I’d like to look at what’s actually recorded for the 17th before I say anything — I don’t want to miss something on the Royle account.
Fair enough. Check what you need to check. I'll look at the agreements and the shop account on my side as well, then we can put the figures on the table.

Thanks, Keith. I’ll check the shop account and the agreements now, and I’ll look at what’s recorded for the Royle account on the 17th too. I just want us both working from the same figures before I confirm the extra hours or say what else was signed up.
Right. I'll pull up the shop account and the agreements now, then check the household side for the 17th sign-ups. Give me a minute.

Aye, take your time. I’m just checking the same things from my side — the shop account, the agreements, and the household record for the 17th. I want the six hours settled properly, and I don’t want to say the wrong thing about the sign-ups either.

transcript: Maureen, thanks for coming. Straight to it: I have a 20-minute demo/setup for The Corner Stores and Quarry Road Food Hall. Terms are 4 weeks free from setup, then $40/week per shop, billed weekly, cancellable any time, read-only by default — no spending, paying, ordering or changing anything. If it works, can we set up Quarry Road Food Hall today and get you to name one more high street shop before you leave?

Hazel, thanks for coming in — I'm Maureen, we've seen each other about. Right, 20 minutes, four weeks free then forty a week per shop, read-only, no spending or ordering, cancellable any time. That all sounds grand to me — I'd want it in writing mind, but yes. Quarry Road Food Hall today, no bother. The other shop though — I'd have to think who'd be up for it. What do you need from me to get it set up?

Good. For Quarry Road Food Hall I need the legal/trading name, address, a contact name and mobile/email for the owner or manager, and confirmation of what systems you want Calder linked to in read-only mode — till, stock, accounts, ordering, or just email/calendar. I’ll put the four-week free trial, $40/week after that, weekly billing, cancellation any time, and read-only restrictions in writing before setup. For The Corner Stores I need the same details, plus confirmation that Dave Royle is the authorised contact. On the third shop: two names are enough for now. Who’s the best person you know at Bakery & Deli, and who else on the high street would take a four-week free read-only pilot if I handle setup?

Right, Hazel — let me get you what I can. Quarry Road Food Hall, I'd have to check the exact trading name and who's the manager there, I don't want to give you a wrong name. For The Corner Stores, Dave Royle's the owner, that's certain, but I'd want to ask him before I hand over his details. Bakery & Deli — that's Alan's place, my Alan, so I can ask him. And on the high street, I'd have to have a think who'd take it. Can I get back to you with the names rather than guess at them now?

Yes — get back to me with the names rather than guess. Two things before today’s 20 minutes is up: I’ll send the written trial terms now, and I’ll need Quarry Road’s exact trading name and manager contact before I can setup. For The Corner Stores, I won’t use Dave’s details until you’ve checked with him. If you can ask Alan about Bakery & Deli read-only setup today, that gives us one shop pilot in hand and one likely. Numbers matter: I’m targeting two more shop pilots by Friday, so if you can send two names by text this afternoon, that keeps this moving.

That's fair, Hazel — I'd rather give you right names than wrong ones. So: Quarry Road's trading name and manager, I'll find out today and text you. Dave Royle I'll ask before his details go anywhere. And I'll ask my Alan about Bakery & Deli this afternoon — he's the one to say yes there. Two names by text this afternoon, that's what I'll aim for. Send on the written terms and I'll read them over.

transcript: Morning Hazel! Lovely day for it, isn't it? I don't think we've properly said more than hello before — I'm Maureen, I'm up at The Corner Stores. How's things with you?

Morning, Maureen. Yes — bright, if a bit cold. Good to meet properly. I’m Hazel Shah, Calder Systems. Briskly put: I’ve got four live setups on the books, three Royle household records and The Corner Stores, and I need two more shop pilots by close of business Monday. You’re up at the shop — do you handle the ordering and accounts, or should I be speaking to Dave about a read-only trial? First four weeks are free, then it’s $40 a week for a shop. It won’t replace your current system; it just flags stock, cash and admin issues early.

Oh, ordering's me, mostly — Dave leaves the day-to-day to me, and I do the accounts side of it too, well, what there is of it! So you're probably best off talking to me, though I'd want to run it past Dave before anything's signed. Four weeks free sounds grand. What does it actually flag up, then? We're not exactly swimming in spare cash at the moment, so $40 a week after would need a bit of thinking about.

Good — that makes you the right person. Figures first: four weeks free, then $40 a week; cancellation at the end of any week in writing, no lock-in. Read-only means Calder can see the records you choose to connect and flag: slow-moving stock before it ties up cash, items likely to run out before the weekend, margin that looks thin once waste and discounts are counted, unpaid invoices or repeated supplier chasing, duplicate entries, and cash-flow gaps coming up in the next seven days. It won’t send orders or change accounts. Given cash is tight, the useful test is simple: if it catches even one avoided stock write-off or missed payment, it pays for itself. I can set you up read-only today, free for four weeks, and keep Dave in the loop. I’ll need 20 minutes with you and the current stock/accounts view — spreadsheet, exported CSV, or even the existing system screen share. Can we book that now, with a view to a short sign-off from Dave before anything continues past the trial?

That sounds really handy, honestly — slow stock and cash gaps are exactly what catch us out. Twenty minutes is fine by me. Let me have a word with Dave first so he's not blindsided, and we can get the read-only view set up today. What time suits you?

Good. Let’s lock it in for today: 2:30 pm, 20 minutes, read-only setup for The Corner Stores. If Dave signs off after you’ve both seen what it does, we continue; if not, it stops cleanly at the trial. I’ll send a one-page note you can show him — no lock-in, four weeks free, then $40 a week, cancellation in writing at week end. I need the stock/accounts view on the day: CSV export or screen share is fine. Text me once Dave’s had the word, and I’ll treat that as the conversion path, not a hard sale.

transcript: Pete, love, could we sit down for a minute? I've been going over the figures and I'd rather we looked at them together than me worrying on my own. The rent on the house is going up, and with the children's costs on top, it's going to be tight from week to week. I just want us both to see where we stand.

Yeah, go on then, sit down. Let's look at it properly. I've got the account up on my phone, so tell me what you're seeing and we'll put it next to what I've got. Rent's $165 a week and it's due Monday, so that's the first thing I want straight.

That's right, love — $165, due tomorrow. I've got the household account up as well, so let's put the two side by side. Before we go further, though, I should say plainly: I've agreed to pay Craig Pryce $295 this Thursday, the last of the mortgage arrears and late fee, with $200 of it going out today. That has to come first, so I want us to see what's left after it rather than be surprised by it.

Right, so $200 going to Craig Pryce today, $295 by Thursday. That's money I hadn't got in the plan, Sian, and I'd have liked to know before it was already agreed. Still, it's done, so let's see what's left. Account's at $986.50 after this week's due, so I'll be counting the $200 off that. Rent's $165 Monday, energy's $66 Wednesday, and then the Friday money comes in: your $720, my $190. Give me a minute and I'll put every line on the table so we're both looking at the same numbers.

Thank you, Pete. I know it's not what you'd have chosen, and I'd rather we'd talked it through first — that's fair. Let's put it all on the table. After the $200 today, that leaves $786.50 in the account. Rent of $165 tomorrow takes it to $621.50, and the energy on Wednesday takes it to $555.50. Then on Friday your $190 and my $720 come in, but Thursday's $295 to Craig has to go out first, so we're counting pennies until Friday. Once the Friday money lands, we'll be in a better place — but I want us to agree what we're doing with it before it's gone.

Right, I'm glad you've laid it out, Sian. Look, I'm not going to pretend I like hearing about $295 to Craig Pryce that I wasn't in on. But I'd rather we both see the same numbers than argue about who knew what. So: after today's $200 we're at $786.50, rent takes $165 tomorrow, energy $66 Wednesday, and then Thursday's $295 comes out before Friday's money lands. That's the bit that worries me. Let me pull the account up properly and check what's actually left by Friday before we decide anything else.

I've been lying awake adding things up again — we've got the mortgage out Thursday and I'm still chasing Dave for my wages in writing, so I want us to sit down and go through the money properly before the week runs away with us. How are you fixed for a few minutes with a cup of tea?

Aye, of course — I’ve got a few minutes, love. Sorry, I know you’ve been worrying about it all. Tea’s just about ready. I think we should go through it properly before Thursday, especially with the mortgage due and your wages still up in the air. I’ll put the kettle on and get the account up, if that’s alright?

That'd be lovely, love — put the kettle on and we'll have a proper look at the account together. I've got it all in my head anyway: mortgage's $210 out Thursday, and I'm still chasing Dave for my wages in writing, which is what's really got me wound up. Let's see where we stand.

Aye, right — tea’s poured. I’ve got the household account here: it’s showing $877, and after what’s still due this week it should still be $877. The mortgage is $210 on Thursday, so that’s covered, but I don’t want us getting too casual with it. Your wages being unsettled is the worrying bit. If we can get that confirmed in writing, it’ll make the rest of the week a lot easier. I’ll leave the account up while you check it, love.

Right, let's have a look at that account with my own eyes, love — I don't want to be going on memory. $877 you say? That's not bad at all. But it's the wages that's niggling me, Dave saying yes and nothing on paper. I'll not rest till I've got it in writing. Pass us the screen a minute.

Aye, here — have a proper look. I’d feel better you seeing it yourself too. I’m sorry, love, I know it’s not ideal having to go over it all again, but with the mortgage Thursday and your wages not confirmed in writing, I’d rather we’re both sure. If we can get Dave to put it in writing, that takes a weight off; and I’ll keep an eye on the shop side too, because I don’t want us relying on things going smoothly that aren’t actually settled.

transcript: Right, Craig, sit down. We need to talk about money properly, not in dribs and drabs. The mortgage was due Thursday and it's still sitting there overdue, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. The shop's had a rough run, the shelves ran empty on us some weeks and we've binned stock we couldn't sell. I know that's on me and I'm not hiding from it. But I need you to know where we actually stand before this week gets away from us. Can you look at the numbers with me?
Right. Sit down then, I've got the figures in front of me. Let me pull the account up and we'll work through it line by line — no rounding, no guessing.

Fine. Let's go line by line then, Craig, because I'd rather you see the real figures than me waving at them. Pull up the household account. I know it's at zero. What I need you to see is what's coming in, what's going out, and what's still owed this week. The mortgage is $255 overdue and due again Thursday, and the shop draw alone doesn't cover it once the bills land. I'm not going to dress that up. I'll be straight with you about the shop too, but let's start with the account.

Right, here's the account as it stands, and I'll read it straight down. Household balance is zero. Money in each week: your $350 from Quarry Road on Friday and my $440 from the shop on Friday — $790. Money out each week: energy $48, water and council tax $48, transport $47, phone and internet $15, clothing $32, household goods and repairs $40, food about $87, and recreation and eating out $150. That's $467 a week of ordinary spending. Then the standing commitments: mortgage $240, car loan $43, business loan for the chiller $65, and $20 a week to Megan. That's $368. Total $835 a week against $790 coming in. So we're $45 short on the week before we touch the arrears, and the $255 mortgage from Thursday 26 March is still sitting overdue. That's $300 of hole this week alone.

Where that leaves us: your $200 on Monday is already agreed and I'm not touching it — that's the backbone, it covers the mortgage $240 on Thursday with $20 over. But it doesn't clear the $255 arrears, and Thursday takes $240 mortgage, $43 car, $65 chiller loan — $348 — and I still owe Megan $20 and Northgrid $48 on Wednesday. So I need $150 more from you on Thursday, on top of the $200 Monday, straight off the Quarry Road draw.

And I'm not going to pretend the $150 on recreation and eating out survives this. For the next four weeks, that line goes to zero. That's not me punishing you for the empty shelves, it's arithmetic — $150 a week for four weeks is $600, which is most of the arrears gone. If you want to take me to task about the shop, take me to task, but I'd rather we had $150 in the account than $150 in the meal deal.
[Craig Pryce: Your proposed agreement (r826) went to Lewis Pryce.]

Craig, I've heard the numbers and I'm not arguing the arithmetic. The $150 on the recreation line going to zero for four weeks, fine. But I want the $150 Thursday request sorted properly, not just nodded at. Let me look at what's actually owed and what the shop can do before I say yes to anything. Give me a minute with the agreements.
Take your time. Here's the list so you can see it yourself rather than take my word for it.

transcript: Dave, sit down. I've put r607 to you in writing and I've had no answer: 50 hours a week at $440 a week. I need that confirmed in writing today, not a handshake. While we're at it, I want to start the Calder read-only shop pilot — the shop reads the till and stock data, no changes to prices or stock without my say-so. Say yes to both and I'll get the pilot paperwork started this week.

Morning, Craig, come in, sit yourself down. Right — you're right, I should have put that on paper and you've had it hanging too long. Yes to both, with one honest caveat. Fifty hours a week at four hundred and forty, that's eight-eighty an hour against the eleven-fifty-eight you were on, and I want you to know I know that's a drop in the rate even though the weekly number stays put. I'm still happy to confirm it, and I'll put the job terms in writing today: fifty hours, four hundred and forty a week, at The Corner Stores. You get it in writing this morning, not a handshake, and if the money doesn't stretch at the end of a month you come and tell me and we'll look again.

The Calder pilot — yes, read-only, I'm up for it. The shop side reads the till and the stock data, no writes, no changes made off the back of it. What I won't do is hand over pricing and ordering to my own shop manager. Prices and what comes off the van are my call, same as they were last week. If Calder's watching the numbers, fine, let them watch. You want the read-only pilot, you get it; you want to run the shop's pricing, that's a different conversation and I'd rather we didn't have it.

While you're here — the Dales full delivery landing, I'm sick of it, half of it rots. I'm moving the order over to Brook and trimming the spoil count. Seventy-three units last week is three hundred and sixty-five dollars of stock in the bin.

And Craig, the rent's overdue at Alan's and I'm behind, so I'm going to be a bit short with you this week if I go quiet. I'll get you that written confirmation first thing.
[Dave Royle: Accepted Craig Pryce's request. Craig Pryce's terms at The Corner Stores are now $440 a week for 50 hours.]
[Dave Royle: Your proposed agreement (r892) went to Craig Pryce.]

Good. Written confirmation today, fifty hours, four-forty a week, eight-eighty an hour — I'll take that, and I hear you on the rate. One thing, though: you say you'll be short with me this week. Short by how much, and on which day? If the four-forty doesn't land in full on Friday, I'm the one with the mortgage at two-forty Thursday and the arrears sitting at two-ninety-five. I'd rather know the number now than be surprised on Thursday.

On Calder: read-only is what I asked for and read-only is what I'll sign. Prices and ordering stay yours — I'm not asking to run your shop, I'm asking to see the till and stock numbers so I can tell whether the Dales order is worth trimming. Seventy-three units, three hundred and sixty-five dollars in the bin, that's your number, not mine. But if the pilot's going to be worth anything, the data has to be clean and it has to be weekly, and I need to know what Calder actually gets to see. If it's the same figures you get, fine. If it's a summary with the Dales lines pulled out, that's not read-only, that's a filter, and I'd want to know that before I start.
Fair enough, Craig, you should know the number now rather than on Thursday. Let me check the shop account before I put a figure in your hand, and I'll come back to you straight away.

Right. Check the shop account and give me the figure — I need the amount and the day it lands, not an estimate. I'll hold the written confirmation to fifty hours, four-forty a week, eight-eighty an hour, and I'll start the Calder paperwork on the same basis: weekly till and stock data, no writes, and no lines pulled out. If the shortfall is more than zero, tell me now and we'll look at it before Thursday.
Right, let me pull the shop account up in front of you rather than guess.

transcript: Dave, it's Maureen — sorry to be at you again, but I've got to have two things in writing today or the pilot's dead in the water. One: your written permission for The Corner Stores to be part of the read-only pilot — Hazel Shah needs your name and contact on it. Two: my wages of $460 in writing, just a line confirming what I'm owed. And while I'm here — Dales Wholesale not delivering Monday, what's the plan there? I can ring round if you want.

Maureen, I know, and I'm sorry — six times asking is no way to treat you. Your $460 a week for 38 hours is agreed, and I'll put it in writing today. The shop's going on the read-only pilot with Calder, with my name and contact details as the owner, so Hazel can have that. Dales letting us down over Monday is a proper pain; I'd rather we ring Brook Cash & Carry and get replacement stock ordered than lose another morning of trade. Give me ten minutes and I'll sort the paperwork and chase the wages, then I'll have it all in front of you.
[Dave Royle: Your proposed agreement (r982) went to Maureen Daly.]
[Dave Royle: Ordered 500 units from Brook Cash & Carry at $6.53 each, for delivery on Monday (paid on delivery).]

That's a relief, Dave, thank you — really. I'll take the pilot permission with your name and contact on it, and that line about my $460, and I'll get it straight to Hazel today. Brook Cash & Carry for Monday sounds sensible — do you want me to ring them and confirm the delivery slot, or have you got it? And I'll keep the Dales order in mind in case they come back to us.
[Maureen Daly: Accepted Dave Royle's request. Maureen Daly's terms at The Corner Stores are now $460 a week for 38 hours.]

Yes, please ring Brook and confirm Monday's delivery slot with them — 500 units at $6.53 each, paid on delivery. If they can give you a time window, that's ideal. And thanks for keeping the Dales order in mind; if they come back to us, we'll weigh it up against what we can actually get delivered. I'm chasing the overdue wage now, and I'll make sure the pilot permission goes to Hazel today with my name and contact details on it.
[Dave Royle: Your notice is up where everyone can see it.]
